newsitem.title: UK: N. Ireland's flashpoint marching season opens.
newsitem.headline: N. Ireland's flashpoint marching season opens.

text.p: Northern Ireland's flashpoint "marching season" of Protestant parades begins on Monday amid signs that extremist sympathisers have abandoned a 29-month truce against Irish nationalist targets.

The British government accused so-called Loyalists of planting a 40-kg (88-lb) car bomb outside a Belfast office of Sinn Fein, the Irish Republican Army's political wing, on Sunday in breach their October 1994 ceasefire.
The bomb, which failed to explode, raised tensions ahead of a month-long series of Protestant parades across the province to display pro-British loyalties in an annual show of allegiance to London.

Last year Northern Ireland suffered its worst civil strife for decades when Protestant and Catholics rioted over a police decision to ban and then allow an Orange Order parade through a Catholic street of the town of Portadown.

Northern Ireland's police chief, Ronnie Flanagan, said he expected "difficulties" in this year's marching season but hoped that people would have learned the lesson of last year's descent to the brink of chaos.
Monday's march is by the Apprentice Boys of Londonderry, an order which traces its origin to a 17th century siege of the town by an invading Catholic king.

The corresponding march last year was marked by violence as police tried to prevent the column passing through a Catholic section of Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road. But this year the order has changed its route to avoid a repetititon.
The marches start as Northern Ireland enters a period of deep uncertainty caused by rising IRA attacks, the apparent breakdown of the Loyalist truce and British elections on May 1.

The political allies of the two main Loyalist guerrilla groups have been allowed to take part in Belfast peace talks by virtue of the Loyalist ceasefire but there will be pressure to expel them if it is deemed to have ended.

A Loyalist source, quoted by the British Broadcasting Corporation, said the attempt to bomb the Sinn Fein office in Belfast's New Lodge Road was a "measured" response to increasing activity by a resurgent IRA.
Weekend IRA attacks included the attempted bombing of a British army patrol on a country road and the shooting by a sniper of a policeman, who suffered a serious leg wound.
Sinn Fein spokesmen said they were encouraged by a Northern Ireland policy statement by the opposition Labour Party, which looks set to win the British elections.
Northern Ireland spokeswoman Mo Mowlam said that if the IRA declared a ceasefire immediately, Sinn Fein could attend the Belfast peace talks when they resumed on June 3.

Her statement did not signal any clear change of policy from that of the Conservative government, which says the IRA must declare a complete end to its 28-year guerrilla war to earn a seat for Sinn Fein at the talks.

Northern Ireland's Protestant Unionist parties, which are usually allied with the Conservatives, say the IRA cannot be trusted and will call only a tactical truce at best while making no move to disarm.
